objects.name: Sun
objects.summary: The star at the centre of the solar system, a ball of hot plasma that holds more than 99.8 percent of the system's mass. Its gravity sets the paths of everything shown here, and its light takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.

objects.name: Mercury
objects.summary: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, so its surface swings from scorching days to freezing nights, and it circles the Sun every 88 days on the most eccentric orbit of the eight planets.

objects.name: Venus
objects.summary: Nearly Earth's twin in size, Venus hides under thick clouds of sulphuric acid above a carbon dioxide atmosphere so dense that the surface is hotter than Mercury's. It spins slowly backwards, so a day there lasts longer than its year.

objects.name: Earth
objects.summary: Our home planet, the third from the Sun and the only world known to carry life. Liquid water covers most of its surface, and its large Moon steadies the tilt of its axis over long spans of time.

objects.name: Moon
objects.summary: Earth's only natural satellite, about a quarter of Earth's diameter. It keeps the same face towards us, raises most of the ocean tides, and is the only other world people have walked on.

objects.name: Mars
objects.summary: A cold desert planet about half Earth's size, red from iron oxide dust. It has the largest volcano and one of the deepest canyons known, polar ice caps, and signs that liquid water once flowed across its surface.

objects.name: Jupiter
objects.summary: The largest planet, a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets together. Its striped clouds and the long-lived Great Red Spot sit above a deep hydrogen interior, and dozens of moons circle it.

objects.name: Saturn
objects.summary: The second largest planet, best known for its broad, bright rings of ice and rock. It is a gas giant less dense than water on average, and its moon Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.

objects.name: Uranus
objects.summary: An ice giant tipped on its side, so each pole spends decades in sunlight and then decades in darkness. Methane in its atmosphere gives it a pale blue-green colour, and faint rings and many small moons surround it.

objects.name: Neptune
objects.summary: The farthest planet from the Sun, an ice giant with the fastest winds measured in the solar system. It takes about 165 years to go round the Sun once, and its largest moon Triton orbits backwards.

objects.name: Voyager 1

status.note: Several instruments switched off to save power; a few still return data.

objects.summary: Launched in 1977 for a tour of Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 flew past both planets and Saturn's moon Titan, then headed out of the plane of the planets. In 2012 it became the first spacecraft to cross into interstellar space, and it is the most distant object people have made.
goals: Study Jupiter, Saturn and their moons and rings
Measure the heliosphere's edge and the interstellar medium

objects.name: Voyager 2

status.note: Several instruments switched off to save power; a few still return data.

objects.summary: The only spacecraft to have visited all four giant planets, Voyager 2 passed Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune between 1979 and 1989. It crossed into interstellar space in 2018, six years after its twin, and still sends back measurements of the space it travels through.
goals: Study the four giant planets, their moons and rings
Measure the heliosphere's edge and the interstellar medium

objects.name: New Horizons
objects.summary: The first mission to Pluto, New Horizons flew past it and its moon Charon in July 2015, revealing nitrogen ice plains and mountains of water ice. On New Year's Day 2019 it passed Arrokoth, a small, two-lobed body in the Kuiper Belt, and it keeps studying the outer solar system on its way out.
goals: Map Pluto and Charon
Explore Kuiper Belt objects
Measure the outer heliosphere

objects.name: Parker Solar Probe
objects.summary: Parker Solar Probe dives through the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, protected by a thick carbon heat shield. Repeated Venus flybys tightened its orbit until, from late 2024, it passes within about 6 million km of the solar surface, faster than any spacecraft before it.
goals: Find out what heats the corona
Trace how the solar wind is accelerated
Study energetic particles near the Sun

objects.name: Juno

status.note: Its extended mission was due to end on 30 September 2025; reports through 2026 show it still flying perijove passes, but its funding status is not stated by NASA.

objects.summary: Juno has orbited Jupiter since July 2016 on long, looping polar orbits that skim low over the cloud tops. Its measurements of gravity and magnetism probe the planet's deep interior, and in its extended mission it has also flown close to the moons Ganymede, Europa and Io.
goals: Measure Jupiter's interior, gravity and magnetic field
Study the atmosphere and polar aurorae
Observe the Galilean moons and the rings

objects.name: Europa Clipper
objects.summary: Europa Clipper is on its way to Jupiter, using flybys of Mars and Earth to gain speed, and is due to arrive in 2030. Once there it will make dozens of close passes of Europa to judge whether the ocean beneath the moon's icy crust could support life.
goals: Measure Europa's ice shell and the ocean beneath it
Study its composition and geology
Look for current activity such as plumes

objects.name: JUICE
objects.summary: The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer is cruising to Jupiter on a path that uses flybys of the Moon, Earth and Venus, with arrival planned for 2031. It will study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa and then become the first spacecraft to orbit a moon of another planet, Ganymede.
goals: Characterise Ganymede, Callisto and Europa as possible habitats
Orbit Ganymede and study its magnetic field
Study Jupiter's atmosphere and magnetosphere

objects.name: Lucy
objects.summary: Lucy is touring the Trojan asteroids, two swarms that share Jupiter's orbit and may be leftovers from the planets' formation. Using Earth flybys to reshape its path, it passed the main-belt asteroids Dinkinesh in 2023 and Donaldjohanson in 2025 and is due to reach its first Trojans in 2027.
goals: Visit several Jupiter Trojan asteroids
Map their surfaces, composition and densities

objects.name: Psyche
objects.summary: Psyche is flying to the asteroid of the same name, a body rich in metal that may be part of the core of an early planet. Driven by electric thrusters and a Mars flyby, it is due to arrive in 2029 and orbit the asteroid to map it.
goals: Find out whether asteroid Psyche is an exposed planetary core
Map its surface, magnetism and composition

objects.name: OSIRIS-APEX
objects.summary: This spacecraft collected a sample from asteroid Bennu as OSIRIS-REx and dropped it off at Earth in 2023. Renamed OSIRIS-APEX, it is now heading for Apophis, which will pass very close to Earth in April 2029, and will study how that encounter changes the asteroid.
goals: Study asteroid Apophis after its 2029 close approach to Earth
Earlier: return a sample of asteroid Bennu

objects.name: LRO
objects.summary: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has circled the Moon in a low orbit since 2009, mapping its surface in great detail. Its maps of terrain, temperature and lighting support the choice of landing sites, and it has photographed the Apollo landing sites from orbit.
goals: Map the Moon's surface at high resolution
Find safe landing sites and possible resources such as ice
Measure the lunar radiation environment

objects.name: CAPSTONE

status.note: NASA's extended mission ended in June 2026; the spacecraft remains in lunar orbit, operated by Advanced Space.

objects.summary: CAPSTONE is a small CubeSat that was the first spacecraft to fly the near-rectilinear halo orbit, a long, stretched path over the Moon's poles chosen for the future Gateway station. It tested navigation and communication methods for that orbit.
goals: Show that a spacecraft can hold a near-rectilinear halo orbit
Test navigation between spacecraft without ground tracking

objects.name: James Webb Space Telescope
objects.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest space telescope yet, with a 6.5 m segmented gold mirror that sees in infrared. It works from a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km beyond Earth, where a large sunshield keeps it cold.
goals: See the first galaxies after the Big Bang
Watch stars and planets form
Study the atmospheres of exoplanets

objects.name: International Space Station
objects.agency: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and CSA
objects.summary: The largest structure people have built in space, crewed without a break since November 2000. It circles Earth about every 92 minutes some 420 km up, on an orbit tilted 51.6 degrees to the equator, so it passes over most of the inhabited world. Its position here is propagated from public orbital elements; it is checked against JPL Horizons' ISS trajectory.
goals: Research in microgravity: biology, materials, human physiology
Preparing for long-duration crewed flights beyond Earth orbit

objects.name: Hubble Space Telescope

status.note: Flying with one gyroscope since 2024 to extend its life; science continues.

objects.summary: A 2.4 m telescope in low Earth orbit about 530 km up, observing in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light above the blur of the atmosphere. Astronauts repaired and upgraded it on five servicing missions; its images and spectra have measured the expansion rate of the universe and the atmospheres of planets around other stars.
goals: Deep imaging of galaxies and the early universe
Spectroscopy of stars, nebulae and exoplanet atmospheres

objects.name: Tiangong
objects.summary: China's modular space station, built around the Tianhe core module launched in 2021 and completed with the Wentian and Mengtian laboratory modules in 2022. It orbits about 390 km up on a 41.5 degree orbit and is crewed by rotating teams of three taikonauts. Its position follows the elements of the Tianhe core.
goals: Long-duration crewed flight and station operations
Experiments in life sciences, materials and fluid physics

objects.name: Starlink-3060

status.note: Status inferred from current orbital elements at operational altitude; SpaceX does not publish per-satellite status.

objects.summary: One of SpaceX's Starlink broadband satellites, from a 2021 launch to the shell about 545 km up on a 70 degree orbit, which covers high latitudes. Starlink is a constellation of thousands of flat-packed satellites that relay internet traffic between user terminals and ground stations, some through laser links between satellites.
goals: Broadband internet from low Earth orbit

objects.name: Starlink-30107

status.note: Status inferred from current orbital elements at operational altitude; SpaceX does not publish per-satellite status.

objects.summary: A second-generation Starlink V2 Mini satellite from an April 2023 launch, flying about 480 km up on a 43 degree orbit. The V2 Mini is larger than the first Starlink design, with bigger solar arrays and laser links to other satellites, so traffic can cross the constellation without a ground station below.
goals: Broadband internet from low Earth orbit

objects.name: Starlink-34343

status.note: Status inferred from current orbital elements at operational altitude; SpaceX does not publish per-satellite status.

objects.summary: A Starlink satellite from a May 2025 launch into a near-polar, Sun-synchronous orbit about 530 km up, tilted 97.6 degrees. Polar shells give coverage at the highest latitudes, where satellites on lower-inclination orbits never pass overhead.
goals: Broadband internet from low Earth orbit

objects.name: GOES-19
objects.summary: The fourth and last of NOAA's GOES-R series weather satellites, in geostationary orbit about 35,786 km above the equator at 75.2 degrees west as GOES-East since April 2025. It watches the Americas and the Atlantic every few minutes, tracking storms and hurricanes, mapping lightning and carrying a coronagraph that sees eruptions leave the Sun.
goals: Continuous weather imaging of the Western Hemisphere
Lightning mapping and space weather monitoring

objects.name: GOES-18
objects.summary: A GOES-R series weather satellite in geostationary orbit at 137.0 degrees west, serving as GOES-West since January 2023. It watches the eastern Pacific, the western United States, Alaska and Hawaii, following wildfires, atmospheric rivers and Pacific storms as they form.
goals: Continuous weather imaging of the eastern Pacific and western Americas
Lightning mapping and fire detection

objects.name: Himawari-9
objects.summary: Japan's geostationary weather satellite at about 140.7 degrees east, the operational Himawari since December 2022. It images the western Pacific, East Asia and Australia every ten minutes, and Japan every two and a half minutes, for typhoon tracking and forecasting.
goals: Weather imaging of East Asia and the western Pacific

objects.name: Meteosat-12
objects.summary: The first Meteosat Third Generation imaging satellite, in geostationary orbit over 0 degrees longitude, where it watches Europe and Africa. It carries a flexible imager that scans the full disc every ten minutes and Europe every two and a half, and the first lightning imager over Europe and Africa.
goals: Weather imaging of Europe and Africa
Lightning detection from geostationary orbit

objects.name: TDRS-13
objects.summary: A Tracking and Data Relay Satellite in geostationary orbit, one of the fleet that relays voice, commands and data between the ground and spacecraft in low Earth orbit, including the International Space Station and Hubble. Relays this high can see a low satellite for most of its orbit, where a ground station sees it only for minutes.
goals: Relay communications for spacecraft in low Earth orbit

objects.name: Landsat 9
objects.summary: The latest satellite of the Landsat programme, which has imaged Earth's land surface continuously since 1972. It flies a Sun-synchronous orbit about 705 km up, crossing the equator at the same local time each morning, and with Landsat 8 revisits every place on Earth every eight days.
goals: Long-term record of land cover, crops, forests, ice and cities

objects.name: NOAA-20
objects.summary: The first satellite of the Joint Polar Satellite System, flying a Sun-synchronous polar orbit about 825 km up and seeing the whole Earth twice a day. Its sounders measure temperature and moisture through the atmosphere, the main input of global weather forecast models.
goals: Global atmospheric soundings for weather forecasts
Imaging of clouds, ice, fires and ocean colour
